Workflow: from Schedule N to merger estimates

Source: vignettes/workflow.Rmd
workflow.Rmd

A study of nonprofit mergers with npmerger has three stages. Each one is a single function, and each writes its tables to one project database.

Stage Function What it builds Reads
1. Mergers build_merger_data() Schedule N labels, merger cases, donor and recipient tables, Part VII rosters, leadership outcomes, typology Schedule N, plus the returns of the organizations involved
2. Matching build_match_data() The full 990 panel, the research sample, the comparison pool, candidates, balance Every 990 and 990-EZ return
3. Model data build_model_data() Treated units, control sets, donor sums, the outcome panel Stages 1 and 2

The models then run from the stage 3 data: merger_did() for the main estimates, did_breakouts(), did_sensitivity(), and did_event_study().

Stage 1 stands on its own. Finding mergers needs only Schedule N and the returns of the organizations that filed it or received assets. If you only want a list of mergers, stop there. Stages 2 and 3 are for comparing merger recipients with organizations that did not merge.

library( npmerger )
library( data.table )

The project folder

merger_project() creates a folder that holds one build:

proj <- merger_project( "~/Documents/NPMERGER" )
NPMERGER/
  PANEL990/          panel990 download cache (reused by later builds)
  npmerger.duckdb    every table, plus build_log and build_settings
  logs/              one log per stage run, <stage>-<time>.log
  results/           model estimates
  README.md          tables, row counts, and the build log

build_merger_database() runs the stages into that folder:

build_merger_database(
  project = proj,
  stages  = c( "merger", "match", "model" ),
  years   = efile_years()
)

A fresh build of every e-file year (2009-2025), run in November 2026:

Stage Time Main tables
merger 54 min on a first run (including the downloads), 42 min once cached 63,706 Schedule N filings; 12,684 merger cases; 1.4 million Part VII person-years
match 7 min 6.2 million organization-years; 3.0 million in the pool; 4,507 treated recipients
model under 1 min 4,507 units; about 75,000 candidate rows per specification; 629,000 organization-years

The download cache is 8 GB and the database 1.6 GB. Running every model in the paper from the model stage takes under a minute.

Each stage reads what it needs from the database, so you can rerun a later stage, for example with different matching calipers, without repeating the earlier ones:

build_merger_database(
  project    = proj,
  stages     = c( "match", "model" ),
  match_args = list( ntee_chars = 3L )
)

Every stage run writes a log with the package versions, git commit, settings, a timestamped line for each step, and sessionInfo(). It also adds a row to the build_log table.

Stage 1: find the mergers

build_merger_data() downloads Schedule N, classifies every filing, and builds the tables about each merger. Here it runs offline on the bundled extract of 2021 filings:

ex <- npmerger_example()

md <-
  build_merger_data(
    sn       = ex$sn,
    evidence = ex$evidence,
    core     = ex$core,
    names    = ex$names,
    bmf_data = ex$bmf,
    ratios   = FALSE,
    verbose  = FALSE
  )

md
#> <merger_data>
#> Schedule N filings by type:
#>   merger2                  8
#>   asset_transfer           6
#>   closure                  6
#>   mergerN                  4
#>   consolidation            4
#>   asset_disposition        1
#> Tables:
#>   cases            16 rows
#>   transfers        16 rows
#>   donors           16 rows
#>   recipients       16 rows
#>   part7          1618 rows
#>   fiscal          166 rows
#>   leadership       11 rows
#>   typology         16 rows

On the full data, the same call takes years and a cache folder instead of the pre-fetched tables:

md <-
  build_merger_data(
    years = efile_years(),
    path  = proj$cache
  )

Two of the tables describe the merger itself rather than the filings:

md$typology[ , .( MERGER_ID, TYPE, TYPOLOGY, RATIO ) ] |> head()
#> Key: <MERGER_ID>
#>                   MERGER_ID          TYPE                        TYPOLOGY
#>                      <char>        <char>                          <fctr>
#> 1: 2021-132890752-861250084 consolidation Consolidation into a new entity
#> 2: 2021-141732612-141670547       merger2 Program or asset-light transfer
#> 3: 2021-232659951-300994771       merger2           Merger of near-equals
#> 4: 2021-263889207-861250084 consolidation Consolidation into a new entity
#> 5: 2021-431339285-436034533       mergerN          Multi-party absorption
#> 6: 2021-454035038-861250084 consolidation Consolidation into a new entity
#>        RATIO
#>        <num>
#> 1:        NA
#> 2: 0.0000000
#> 3: 0.7784352
#> 4:        NA
#> 5: 0.5011514
#> 6:        NA

md$leadership records what happened to the two chief executives and the two boards (merger_leadership()). It needs rosters on both sides of the merger, so it is empty for this one-year extract.

Stage 2: build the comparison data

build_match_data() reads every 990 filer into one panel and finds comparison organizations for each merger recipient. See vignette("matching") for the design. The rest of this page uses a simulated panel of 600 organizations, 30 of which absorb another organization in 2015 and grow by about 30% afterwards.

mm <-
  build_match_data(
    merger_data = sim,
    panel       = panel,
    verbose     = FALSE
  )

mm
#> <merger_match_data>
#>   panel:     5,400 org-years
#>   sample:    30 cases, 30 treated units
#>   pool:      2,862 org-years
#>   margin:    30 of 30 treated matched, median 394 candidates
#>   equity:    30 of 30 treated matched, median 229.5 candidates

On the full data, leave out panel and give the cache folder. The panel is built from the same files stage 1 downloaded:

mm <- build_match_data( md, path = proj$cache )

Stage 3: assemble the model data

build_model_data() does the slow joins once. It keeps one row per treated recipient with its breakout variables, the closest candidate controls for every matching specification (plus a match on the combined recipient and donor baseline), donor sums for the pro forma outcomes, and only the organization-years the models read.

dd <- build_model_data( sim, mm, verbose = FALSE )

dd
#> <merger_model_data>
#>   units:      30 treated recipients (30 without other mergers in the window)
#>   r_margin:   584 candidate rows
#>   r_equity:   587 candidate rows
#>   c_margin:   575 candidate rows
#>   panel:      3,029 org-years
#>   limits:     k <= 10, year gap <= 2

max_k and max_year_gap set the largest control sets and calendar-year gaps any later model can ask for (10 and 2 by default).

Run the models

Every model reads only dd. merger_did() gives long-difference estimates, from two years before the merger to two years after, for each design:

fit <-
  merger_did(
    data     = dd,
    outcomes = c( "LOG_REVENUE", "MARGIN" ),
    keep     = NULL
  )

fit[ , .( design, outcome, estimate, se, n_sets ) ] |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 3 )
design outcome estimate se n_sets
naive | recipient match LOG_REVENUE 0.261 0.030 30
naive | recipient match MARGIN 0.021 0.009 30
proforma | recipient match LOG_REVENUE -0.527 0.134 30
proforma | recipient match MARGIN 0.018 0.011 30
proforma | combined match LOG_REVENUE -0.548 0.137 30
proforma | combined match MARGIN 0.009 0.011 30

keep = NULL uses every treated unit. The default, ~ OTHER == FALSE, drops recipients involved in other mergers in the window.

The three designs are listed by did_designs(). The recipient alone grows by about the simulated 30% (0.26 log points). The pro forma designs compare the merged organization with the recipient and donor combined before the merger. In this simulation the donors are about as large as their recipients, but the recipients grow by only 30%, so the merged organization ends up smaller than the two were apart and the pro forma estimates are negative.

Breakouts

Interact treatment with any unit-level variable from did_breakout_vars():

br <-
  did_breakouts(
    data     = dd,
    by       = "AFFILIATED",
    outcomes = "LOG_REVENUE",
    designs  = "naive | recipient match",
    keep     = NULL
  )

br[ , .( spec, term, estimate, se ) ] |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 3 )
spec term estimate se
pooled 0.261 0.030
AFFILIATED AFFILIATEDFALSE 0.228 0.043
AFFILIATED AFFILIATEDTRUE 0.295 0.038

Sensitivity

did_variants() lists the paper’s variants. Each is a set of merger_did() arguments, so adding one is a single line:

v <- did_variants()[ c( "base", "k1", "gap2" ) ]

# use every unit in this small example
v <- lapply( v, modifyList, list( keep = ~ TRUE ) )

# one more: three controls per recipient
v$k3 <- modifyList( v$base, list( k = 3L ) )

sens <-
  did_sensitivity(
    data     = dd,
    variants = v,
    outcomes = "LOG_REVENUE",
    designs  = "naive | recipient match"
  )

sens[ , .( variant, estimate, se, n_sets ) ] |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 3 )
variant estimate se n_sets
base 0.261 0.030 30
k1 0.241 0.042 30
gap2 0.248 0.046 30
k3 0.251 0.031 30

Event study 

es <-
  did_event_study(
    data     = dd,
    outcomes = "LOG_REVENUE",
    designs  = "naive | recipient match",
    keep     = NULL
  )

es[ , .( E, estimate, se ) ] |>
  knitr::kable( digits = 3 )
E estimate se
-3 0.002 0.027
-1 0.049 0.035
0 0.286 0.034
1 0.272 0.031
2 0.261 0.030

did_baseline_means(), did_funnel(), and did_composition() describe the same samples: outcome means at t-2, the counts from merger cases to the units and controls used, and the treated units in each breakout group.

Coming back to a project

Everything is in the database, so a later session starts from load_model_data() instead of rebuilding:

proj <- merger_project( "~/Documents/NPMERGER" )

dd  <- load_model_data( proj )
fit <- merger_did( dd )

load_merger_data() and load_match_data() return the stage 1 and stage 2 objects, and db_read() reads any single table:

db_tables( proj )

db_read( proj, "match_balance" )
